**Section 5 – Safety, Trust and User Protection**

**5.1 Overview**

Trust and safety remain foundational to Coastal Exchange’s operations. During 2024 we continued to invest in protections for buyers and sellers, with a focus on reducing harm from scams, improving response times for reports, and deepening our cooperation with regulators and law enforcement. This section summarises our safety initiatives, the protocols that govern them, and the collaborations that support them.

**5.2 Safety protocols and platform controls**

Our safety framework is built around prevention, detection, and response. The principal components are described below.

*Account verification.* All sellers are required to complete identity verification before listing items. Buyers may transact without verification, but unverified buyers are subject to transaction limits and additional payment safeguards. During 2024 we introduced optional two-factor authentication for all accounts; take-up currently stands at 41% of active accounts.

*Listing screening.* Every listing is screened at the point of upload against a set of automated rules covering prohibited goods, restricted categories, and known scam signatures. Listings that fall outside these rules are flagged for manual review. In 2024, the automated screening process reviewed over 2.1 million listings. Manual review was required for approximately 3% of those.

*Payment protections.* We continue to encourage the use of the platform’s recommended payment methods, which provide both buyer and seller protections. Transactions conducted through external channels, including direct bank transfer, are not covered by these protections. Our Buyer Protection Program, described in Section 4.3, applies only to purchases made and paid for on the platform.

*Data security.* We maintain a documented information security program aligned with the Australian Privacy Principles. Access to user data is restricted by role, and all access is logged and reviewed on a quarterly basis. In 2024 we completed a scheduled external audit of our security controls; no material deficiencies were identified.

**5.3 User education and awareness**

We operate a year-round user education program aimed at helping members recognise and avoid common scams. The program includes:

- In-app notifications that warn buyers about risky payment requests, including requests to move conversations off-platform.
- A dedicated safety hub on the Coastal Exchange website, with plain-language guides on phishing, payment fraud, and counterfeit goods.
- Quarterly email campaigns targeting high-risk user segments, such as new sellers and buyers of high-value electronics.
- Partnering with a community legal centre to produce fact sheets on consumer rights and dispute resolution.

During 2024 we also piloted a short interactive quiz on scam recognition, delivered through the app. The quiz was completed by 3,240 users. We are reviewing the results to determine whether the quiz should be offered more broadly in 2025.

**5.4 Collaboration with authorities**

Coastal Exchange works with a range of government agencies and industry bodies to combat online fraud and scams. Our cooperation includes:

- Reporting of suspected scams to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) through the Scamwatch reporting portal.
- Referral of cases involving suspected criminal activity to the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and state and territory police, as appropriate.
- Participation in the Australian Banking Association’s industry working group on payment scams, where we share de-identified trend data with other platforms and financial institutions.
- Regular liaison with the Office of the eSafety Commissioner on matters relating to online safety and harmful content.
**5.5 Community engagement and outreach**

Beyond our formal partnerships with regulators and law enforcement, Coastal Exchange invests in community-level engagement to build digital literacy and scam resilience among consumers and small businesses. Our outreach during 2024 and the first half of 2025 focused on reaching groups that are disproportionately affected by online scams, including older Australians, culturally and linguistically diverse communities, and regional and remote sellers.

**Consumer advocacy partnerships**

We continued our relationship with the Consumer Action Law Centre (CALC), which began in 2023, to co-produce plain-language resources on consumer rights when buying and selling online. During 2024, CALC and Coastal Exchange jointly published a revised edition of the *Buying and Selling Safely* fact sheet series. The series covers topics such as:

- How to identify a suspicious payment request.
- What to do if a buyer or seller asks you to pay by gift card or cryptocurrency.
- Your rights under the Australian Consumer Law when a purchase is faulty or not as described.
- How to escalate a dispute through Coastal Exchange’s resolution process, including timeframes and what documentation to keep.

The revised fact sheets were distributed through our safety hub, through CALC’s network of community legal centres, and at in-person events. We printed 10,000 copies of the most popular titles for distribution at libraries, neighbourhood houses, and seniors’ clubs in Victoria and New South Wales. A digital version was made available to all users through the app, and we recorded 18,400 downloads of the fact sheet series between January and December 2024.

**Community legal centre workshops**

In partnership with a consortium of community legal centres coordinated by CALC, we delivered a series of in-person and online workshops titled *Staying Safe on Marketplace Apps*. The workshops were designed for older adults and for people who are new to online selling. Between March 2024 and June 2025, we held 34 workshops across Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, and Western Australia. Attendance totalled 1,180 participants. Feedback collected after each session indicated that 92% of participants felt more confident identifying scam attempts after attending.

Workshop content included live demonstrations of common scam techniques, such as fake payment confirmation emails and overpayment scams, and practical guidance on how to use Coastal Exchange’s reporting tools. We also invited local police cybercrime officers to attend several sessions, which allowed participants to ask questions about how to report scams to authorities.

**Regional and remote outreach**

Recognising that users in regional and remote areas may have less access to face-to-face support, we piloted a targeted outreach program in 2024. The pilot focused on the Northern Territory, Tasmania, and regional Queensland. Activities included:

- A partnership with the Rural Financial Counselling Service to include scam awareness materials in their regular client communications.
- Two radio segments broadcast on community radio stations in Darwin and Cairns, in which our safety team discussed common marketplace scams and how to avoid them.
- A series of short videos, produced with the assistance of a community legal centre, that were shared through local Facebook groups and rural trader networks.

The pilot concluded in December 2024. Based on survey responses from 214 participants, we found that awareness of how to report a scam to Scamwatch increased from 41% before the program to 68% after. We are considering how to extend the program to other regions in 2025–26, subject to budget approval.

Subject: Beware of Fake Shipping Notifications – Follow-Up to 3 February Notice

This notice follows our earlier warning of 3 February 2025 regarding fraudulent shipping notifications sent to Coastal Exchange members. Since that notice, we have seen a change in the way these scams are being delivered, and we want to make sure you have the latest information.

What has changed

In the past fortnight, scammers have moved beyond simple email and SMS. We are now seeing fake shipping notifications delivered through:

- Social media direct messages, including messages that appear to come from Coastal Exchange’s official Facebook and Instagram accounts.
- QR codes printed on paper slips left in letterboxes. These slips claim a parcel could not be delivered and ask you to scan the code to reschedule.
- Phone calls from numbers that appear to be Australian mobile numbers. In some cases, the caller claims to be from Coastal Exchange’s delivery partner and asks you to confirm your address or payment details.

These methods are designed to look more convincing than the earlier email-based scams. The QR code slips, in particular, have been reported in several suburbs across Sydney and Melbourne. If you receive one of these slips, do not scan the code. Coastal Exchange does not leave paper slips for undelivered parcels. Our delivery partners will either leave a card with their own logo and contact details, or they will contact you through the Coastal Exchange app.

New verification protocols

As part of our ongoing response, Coastal Exchange has introduced new verification protocols for all account-related communications. These protocols came into effect on 10 February 2025.

1. All official Coastal Exchange emails now include a verification code in the subject line. This code is unique to each message and can be checked in the Security section of your account settings.

2. SMS messages from Coastal Exchange will never include a link. Instead, they will direct you to log in to your account to view any updates. If you receive an SMS that includes a link and claims to be from Coastal Exchange, it is a scam.

3. Phone calls from Coastal Exchange support staff will always come from a verified number. You can see a list of verified numbers in the Security section of your account. If you receive a call from a number not on this list, hang up and contact us directly.

4. QR codes are no longer used in any Coastal Exchange communication. If you see a QR code on anything that claims to be from Coastal Exchange, it is fraudulent.

These protocols were developed in consultation with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) and Scamwatch, and we encourage you to familiarise yourself with them.

What we are doing

Since the 3 February notice, we have:

- Removed more than 120 fraudulent listings that were linked to the shipping notification scam.
- Worked with two Australian courier companies to identify and block phone numbers used by scammers.
- Added new automated checks that flag accounts which receive a high volume of shipping-related messages in a short period.

We are also working with the Australian Federal Police on a small number of cases where members have reported significant financial losses. These cases are ongoing, and we are unable to provide further details at this time.

What you should do now

Even if you have not received a suspicious message, we recommend taking the following steps:

- Review the security settings on your Coastal Exchange account. Make sure your recovery email and phone number are up to date.
- If you have not already enabled two-factor authentication (2FA), do this now. You can find this option under Account Settings > Security.
- Check your saved payment methods and remove any that you no longer use.
- Talk to family members, particularly older relatives, about the QR code slip scam. We have received reports that these slips are being left at homes where older Australians live.

"People told us they wanted something they could print out and keep by their computer," Sharma said. "So we've made it very practical. It tells you exactly what to look for, step by step."

The guide lists several red flags that have appeared repeatedly in local reports. These include buyers who insist on using the platform's EasyShip service but then claim the parcel never arrived, tracking numbers that show collection within an hour of the order being placed, and accounts that were created only days before the purchase.

It also advises sellers to photograph or video every parcel before collection, to keep all messages within the platform's chat function, and to request signature on delivery where the service allows it.

**Local reactions mixed**

Residents who spoke to the Bulletin after the guide's launch said they welcomed the information but questioned whether it would be enough.

**Section 5 – Safety, Trust and User Protection**

**5.1 Overview**

Trust and safety remain foundational to Coastal Exchange’s operations. During 2024 we continued to invest in protections for buyers and sellers, with a focus on reducing harm from scams, improving response times for reports, and deepening our cooperation with regulators and law enforcement. This section summarises our safety initiatives, the protocols that govern them, and the collaborations that support them.

**5.2 Safety protocols and platform controls**

Our safety framework is built around prevention, detection, and response. The principal components are described below.

*Account verification.* All sellers are required to complete identity verification before listing items. Buyers may transact without verification, but unverified buyers are subject to transaction limits and additional payment safeguards. During 2024 we introduced optional two-factor authentication for all accounts; take-up currently stands at 41% of active accounts.

*Listing screening.* Every listing is screened at the point of upload against a set of automated rules covering prohibited goods, restricted categories, and known scam signatures. Listings that fall outside these rules are flagged for manual review. In 2024, the automated screening process reviewed over 2.1 million listings. Manual review was required for approximately 3% of those.

*Payment protections.* We continue to encourage the use of the platform’s recommended payment methods, which provide both buyer and seller protections. Transactions conducted through external channels, including direct bank transfer, are not covered by these protections. Our Buyer Protection Program, described in Section 4.3, applies only to purchases made and paid for on the platform.

*Data security.* We maintain a documented information security program aligned with the Australian Privacy Principles. Access to user data is restricted by role, and all access is logged and reviewed on a quarterly basis. In 2024 we completed a scheduled external audit of our security controls; no material deficiencies were identified.

**5.3 User education and awareness**

We operate a year-round user education program aimed at helping members recognise and avoid common scams. The program includes:

- In-app notifications that warn buyers about risky payment requests, including requests to move conversations off-platform.
- A dedicated safety hub on the Coastal Exchange website, with plain-language guides on phishing, payment fraud, and counterfeit goods.
- Quarterly email campaigns targeting high-risk user segments, such as new sellers and buyers of high-value electronics.
- Partnering with a community legal centre to produce fact sheets on consumer rights and dispute resolution.

During 2024 we also piloted a short interactive quiz on scam recognition, delivered through the app. The quiz was completed by 3,240 users. We are reviewing the results to determine whether the quiz should be offered more broadly in 2025.

**5.4 Collaboration with authorities**

Coastal Exchange works with a range of government agencies and industry bodies to combat online fraud and scams. Our cooperation includes:

- Reporting of suspected scams to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) through the Scamwatch reporting portal.
- Referral of cases involving suspected criminal activity to the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and state and territory police, as appropriate.
- Participation in the Australian Banking Association’s industry working group on payment scams, where we share de-identified trend data with other platforms and financial institutions.
- Regular liaison with the Office of the eSafety Commissioner on matters relating to online safety and harmful content.

**5.5 Community engagement and outreach**

Beyond our formal partnerships with regulators and law enforcement, Coastal Exchange invests in community-level engagement to build digital literacy and scam resilience among consumers and small businesses. Our outreach during 2024 and the first half of 2025 focused on reaching groups that are disproportionately affected by online scams, including older Australians, culturally and linguistically diverse communities, and regional and remote sellers.

**Consumer advocacy partnerships**

We continued our relationship with the Consumer Action Law Centre (CALC), which began in 2023, to co-produce plain-language resources on consumer rights when buying and selling online. During 2024, CALC and Coastal Exchange jointly published a revised edition of the *Buying and Selling Safely* fact sheet series. The series covers topics such as:

- How to identify a suspicious payment request.
- What to do if a buyer or seller asks you to pay by gift card or cryptocurrency.
- Your rights under the Australian Consumer Law when a purchase is faulty or not as described.
- How to escalate a dispute through Coastal Exchange’s resolution process, including timeframes and what documentation to keep.

The revised fact sheets were distributed through our safety hub, through CALC’s network of community legal centres, and at in-person events. We printed 10,000 copies of the most popular titles for distribution at libraries, neighbourhood houses, and seniors’ clubs in Victoria and New South Wales. A digital version was made available to all users through the app, and we recorded 18,400 downloads of the fact sheet series between January and December 2024.

**Community legal centre workshops**

In partnership with a consortium of community legal centres coordinated by CALC, we delivered a series of in-person and online workshops titled *Staying Safe on Marketplace Apps*. The workshops were designed for older adults and for people who are new to online selling. Between March 2024 and June 2025, we held 34 workshops across Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, and Western Australia. Attendance totalled 1,180 participants. Feedback collected after each session indicated that 92% of participants felt more confident identifying scam attempts after attending.

Workshop content included live demonstrations of common scam techniques, such as fake payment confirmation emails and overpayment scams, and practical guidance on how to use Coastal Exchange’s reporting tools. We also invited local police cybercrime officers to attend several sessions, which allowed participants to ask questions about how to report scams to authorities.

**Regional and remote outreach**

Recognising that users in regional and remote areas may have less access to face-to-face support, we piloted a targeted outreach program in 2024. The pilot focused on the Northern Territory, Tasmania, and regional Queensland. Activities included:

- A partnership with the Rural Financial Counselling Service to include scam awareness materials in their regular client communications.
- Two radio segments broadcast on community radio stations in Darwin and Cairns, in which our safety team discussed common marketplace scams and how to avoid them.
- A series of short videos, produced with the assistance of a community legal centre, that were shared through local Facebook groups and rural trader networks.

The pilot concluded in December 2024. Based on survey responses from 214 participants, we found that awareness of how to report a scam to Scamwatch increased from 41% before the program to 68% after. We are considering how to extend the program to other regions in 2025–26, subject to budget approval.

**User Base and Marketplace Activity**

As at 31 December 2023, Coastal Exchange had 4.7 million registered users, an increase of 14.6% from 4.1 million at the end of 2022. Of these, 2.9 million were classified as active users, defined as having logged in at least once in the preceding 90 days. Active users grew by 16.0% year-on-year.

The number of active listings on the platform averaged 1.8 million per month during 2023, up from 1.5 million in 2022. Gross merchandise value (GMV) transacted through the platform reached $2.1 billion, compared to $1.7 billion in the prior year, representing growth of 23.5%.

New user registrations totalled 1.2 million in 2023. We observed a notable increase in registrations from users aged 55 and over, who now account for 24% of new sign-ups, up from 19% in 2022. This trend aligns with the uptake of our community workshops, which were particularly well-attended by older adults.

**Scam and Safety Reporting**

During 2023, we received 18,432 reports of suspected scams or fraudulent activity from users. This represented a 12% increase on the 16,458 reports received in 2022. The increase is partially attributable to greater awareness of reporting tools following our education campaigns, as well as a genuine rise in scam attempts observed across the broader Australian online marketplace sector.

Of the reports received in 2023, 7,891 were classified as confirmed scams following investigation, and 4,203 were escalated to law enforcement agencies. The remaining reports were closed as either false positives or resolved through our dispute resolution process. We note that figures for the final quarter of 2023 are still pending verification by our internal audit team and may be subject to minor adjustment.

The most common scam types reported during the year were:

- Payment outside the platform (fake payment confirmations): 34% of confirmed scams
- Overpayment and refund scams: 22%
- Goods not received after payment: 18%
- Fake or misrepresented goods: 15%

The following statements are made as at 30 June 2025 and are based on information available to the Board at that date. These statements are provided in accordance with the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) and the ASX Corporate Governance Council's Principles and Recommendations. Readers are cautioned that forward-looking statements involve inherent risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied.

### Strategic Priorities for 2025–2027

The Board has approved a three-year strategic plan with four principal pillars:

1. **Trust and Safety Infrastructure Modernisation** – Allocation of $18 million over three years for the upgrade of detection systems, expansion of the Trust and Safety team, and development of a dedicated incident response capability. This program commenced in March 2025 with the appointment of a Chief Trust and Safety Officer, a position newly created following recommendations from the 2024 independent review (see Section 9.4 of this report for the review's findings).

2. **Regulatory Engagement** – Continued liaison with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), the Office of the eSafety Commissioner, and state-based fair trading agencies. We will participate in the ACCC's Digital Platform Services Inquiry as it relates to online marketplaces, and we intend to make a submission to the Treasury's consultation on the proposed Scam Code of Practice, anticipated to apply from late 2025.

3. **Regional Expansion** – A pilot of an expanded logistics booking service to be launched in South Australia and Western Australia in the second half of 2025, subject to final regulatory clearance. This service is designed to complement our existing seller tools.

4. **User Education** – Expansion of the Community Workshop program, with a target of 400 sessions delivered in 2025–26, up from 312 sessions in 2024. Specific modules on safe payment methods and recognising phishing attempts will be added, based on user feedback and scam-report data described in Section 5.

The Board notes that these statements are subject to change as market conditions and regulatory requirements evolve. No assurance is given that the outcomes described will be achieved.

### Regulatory and Compliance Updates

**Scam Code of Practice.** In April 2025, the Government released a draft Scam Code of Practice for public consultation. The draft code, which would apply to banks, telecommunications providers, and digital platforms including online marketplaces, sets out minimum standards for scam detection, prevention, and response. We have reviewed the draft and have provided a submission to Treasury in June 2025. Key elements of our submission include:

- Support for a risk-based approach to scam detection rather than a prescriptive list of prohibited transactions;
- A request for clarification on the interaction between the code and existing obligations under the Australian Consumer Law;
- Recommendations that the code recognise the distinct risk profiles of different marketplace categories, particularly consumer-to-consumer platforms.

We have also engaged with the Consumer Action Law Centre and the Financial Rights Legal Centre in preparing our submission. The final code is expected to be released in late 2025, with a proposed commencement date of mid-2026. We will report to shareholders on the implications of the final code in the 2026 annual report.

**eSafety Commissioner Engagement.** In February 2025, we concluded a voluntary information-sharing arrangement with the eSafety Commissioner relating to reports of harmful image-based content on our platform. Under this arrangement, we provide de-identified data on the volume and nature of such reports on a quarterly basis. The first data exchange under this arrangement occurred in May 2025. We regard this as a constructive relationship and expect it to continue.

What we have seen so far
Reports of this scam have increased over the last two weeks. As of the date of this notice, we have received 47 reports from members who received a fake shipping notification. Of those, 12 members confirmed that they clicked the link and entered their details. Seven of those members reported unauthorised activity on their accounts. The remaining reports are still pending verification, and we are working with affected members to secure their accounts.

We are also aware of at least three variations of the scam message. The most common variation asks you to pay a small "redelivery fee." Another variation claims that a package is being held at customs and asks you to provide personal identification. A third variation targets sellers, claiming that a buyer's payment is on hold until the seller "confirms shipping" by clicking a link.

What Coastal Exchange is doing
We have taken the following steps to address this scam:

- Removed known phishing links from messages sent through the Coastal Exchange platform.
- Added warnings to member accounts that have been flagged as potentially compromised.
- Contacted the affected members directly with instructions on how to secure their accounts.
- Reported the phishing domains to the relevant authorities, including the Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) and the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) via Scamwatch.
- Increased automated monitoring for messages that contain suspicious links or that ask members to move conversations off the platform.

Please note that our previous notice about phishing scams, issued in September 2024, contained advice about a different scam involving fake payment confirmations. Some of the advice in that notice still applies, but the current scam is specifically about shipping notifications. The safest approach is to follow the steps below for any unsolicited message.

How to protect yourself
- Do not click links in unsolicited emails, SMS messages, or social media messages, even if they appear to come from Coastal Exchange or a courier company.
- Always go directly to the Coastal Exchange website or app by typing the address into your browser or using your saved bookmark. Never use a link from a message.
- Check the sender's email address or phone number carefully. Scammers often use addresses that look similar to legitimate ones, such as "support@coastaI-exchange.com" (with a capital I instead of a lowercase l) or "auspost-delivery@outlook.com".
- Coastal Exchange will never ask you for your password, your full credit card number, or your one-time SMS code. If a message asks for any of these, it is a scam.
- If you receive a shipping notification that you were not expecting, contact the courier company directly using the contact details on their official website.
- Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) on your Coastal Exchange account. This adds an extra layer of protection even if your password is compromised.

What to do if you think you have been affected
If you clicked a link in a suspicious message and entered your details, or if you believe your account has been accessed by someone else, take the following steps immediately:

1. Change your Coastal Exchange password. You can do this by going to Account Settings > Security.
2. If you cannot log in, use the "Forgot password" option. If that does not work, contact our support team using the details below.
3. Check your account for any unauthorised messages, purchases, or changes to your payment methods.
4. Review your recent transactions on any payment method you have saved on the platform.
5. If you entered your credit card details on a phishing page, contact your bank or card issuer immediately to report the possible fraud.
6. Report the scam to Scamwatch at scamwatch.gov.au. This helps the ACCC track scam trends and warn others.

documents.content:
Coastal Exchange
Public Notice
Issued 14 February 2025
Subject: Beware of Fake Shipping Notifications – Follow-Up to 3 February Notice

This notice follows our earlier warning of 3 February 2025 regarding fraudulent shipping notifications sent to Coastal Exchange members. Since that notice, we have seen a change in the way these scams are being delivered, and we want to make sure you have the latest information.

What has changed

In the past fortnight, scammers have moved beyond simple email and SMS. We are now seeing fake shipping notifications delivered through:

- Social media direct messages, including messages that appear to come from Coastal Exchange’s official Facebook and Instagram accounts.
- QR codes printed on paper slips left in letterboxes. These slips claim a parcel could not be delivered and ask you to scan the code to reschedule.
- Phone calls from numbers that appear to be Australian mobile numbers. In some cases, the caller claims to be from Coastal Exchange’s delivery partner and asks you to confirm your address or payment details.

These methods are designed to look more convincing than the earlier email-based scams. The QR code slips, in particular, have been reported in several suburbs across Sydney and Melbourne. If you receive one of these slips, do not scan the code. Coastal Exchange does not leave paper slips for undelivered parcels. Our delivery partners will either leave a card with their own logo and contact details, or they will contact you through the Coastal Exchange app.

New verification protocols

As part of our ongoing response, Coastal Exchange has introduced new verification protocols for all account-related communications. These protocols came into effect on 10 February 2025.

1. All official Coastal Exchange emails now include a verification code in the subject line. This code is unique to each message and can be checked in the Security section of your account settings.

2. SMS messages from Coastal Exchange will never include a link. Instead, they will direct you to log in to your account to view any updates. If you receive an SMS that includes a link and claims to be from Coastal Exchange, it is a scam.

3. Phone calls from Coastal Exchange support staff will always come from a verified number. You can see a list of verified numbers in the Security section of your account. If you receive a call from a number not on this list, hang up and contact us directly.

4. QR codes are no longer used in any Coastal Exchange communication. If you see a QR code on anything that claims to be from Coastal Exchange, it is fraudulent.

These protocols were developed in consultation with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) and Scamwatch, and we encourage you to familiarise yourself with them.

What we are doing

Since the 3 February notice, we have:

- Removed more than 120 fraudulent listings that were linked to the shipping notification scam.
- Worked with two Australian courier companies to identify and block phone numbers used by scammers.
- Added new automated checks that flag accounts which receive a high volume of shipping-related messages in a short period.

We are also working with the Australian Federal Police on a small number of cases where members have reported significant financial losses. These cases are ongoing, and we are unable to provide further details at this time.

What you should do now

Even if you have not received a suspicious message, we recommend taking the following steps:

- Review the security settings on your Coastal Exchange account. Make sure your recovery email and phone number are up to date.
- If you have not already enabled two-factor authentication (2FA), do this now. You can find this option under Account Settings > Security.
- Check your saved payment methods and remove any that you no longer use.
- Talk to family members, particularly older relatives, about the QR code slip scam. We have received reports that these slips are being left at homes where older Australians live.

One of those sellers is Rachel Nguyen of Sandringham, who sold a vintage record player for $220 on 3 November. Ms Nguyen said she had been selling on the platform for six years and had never had a problem until last month.

"I had a buyer message me asking if I could use EasyShip because they'd had a parcel stolen from their letterbox before and wanted the signature-on-delivery option," Ms Nguyen said. "I thought it was a reasonable request, so I selected the premium label, paid the extra $4.50, and posted it the next day from the Moorabbin post office."

Ms Nguyen said the tracking showed the parcel had been collected from the post office on 6 November, but the buyer opened a dispute on 8 November claiming it had never arrived.

"The platform's automated system sent me a message saying the tracking number didn't match the delivery address, and they refunded the buyer within 24 hours. I tried to appeal, but the form just kept telling me I needed to upload a proof-of-delivery photo, which doesn't exist for a post office collection."

A second seller, who asked not to be named because she feared retaliation from the buyer, described an almost identical experience with a $140 winter coat sold on 9 November.

"It's the same script every time," she said. "They ask for EasyShip, they ask for the most expensive label, they wait for the parcel to be collected, and then they dispute it. By the time you've appealed, the money is already back in their account and the platform has closed the case."

The Bulletin contacted the marketplace platform, which operates under the name "BayMarket" in Australia, for comment. A spokesperson said the company was aware of the reports and had opened an investigation.

"We take the security of our marketplace seriously," the spokesperson said in a written statement. "We have dedicated teams investigating reports of fraudulent activity, and we have recently updated our dispute resolution process to include a manual review step for high-value claims. Sellers who believe they have been affected should contact our support team directly."

The spokesperson did not respond to follow-up questions about how many refunds had been issued in the affected cases, nor whether the platform would reimburse sellers whose disputes were found to be fraudulent.

Local consumer advocate Peter Mastroianni, who runs a small business advisory service in Hampton, said the platform's response was "too little, too late" for the sellers already out of pocket.

"The platform is acting as both the payment processor and the dispute arbiter, and that's a conflict of interest," Mr Mastroianni said. "They have the tracking data. They can see the parcel was collected. Yet they're still siding with the buyer in these disputes. It's a design flaw that these scammers have figured out and are exploiting at scale."

Mr Mastroianni said sellers should be wary of any buyer who specifically requests EasyShip, particularly for higher-value items.

"Ask yourself why a buyer would care how you post something," he said. "If they're asking for a specific label service, that's a red flag. Take photos of the item before you pack it, film yourself at the post office counter if you can, and keep every receipt. You need a paper trail that goes beyond what the platform provides."

The Bulletin has also viewed screenshots of a private Facebook group where at least three local sellers have shared their experiences. The posts follow a similar pattern: a buyer with a recently created account, a request for EasyShip, a dispute opened within days of the parcel being collected, and a refund approved by the platform's automated system.

"The tracking is the single point of failure," said Dr. Meera Iyer, a cybersecurity researcher at RMIT who has studied online marketplace fraud. "The platform is treating the carrier's scan events as the authoritative record. But if a scammer can cause a delay in that record, or if the platform's integration with the carrier is slow to update, the seller loses the benefit of the evidence they actually have."

Dr. Iyer said she had seen similar schemes in other countries, where fraudsters exploit the gap between the physical scan and the digital record. "It's not that the carrier is lying," she said. "It's that the platform's dispute system is designed for speed, not for accuracy. A human reviewer would look at the seller's receipt and see the parcel was collected. The automated system just sees an incomplete data feed and makes a decision."

The Bulletin obtained a copy of the platform's seller dispute policy, dated January 2025, which states that "tracking information provided by the carrier is the primary evidence used to determine the outcome of a dispute." The policy also notes that "sellers may submit additional evidence, such as receipts or photos, but this evidence will only be considered if the dispute is escalated to manual review."

A spokesperson for the platform declined to say how many disputes are escalated to manual review, or what percentage of escalated disputes result in a refund for the seller. In response to questions about the January policy, the spokesperson said: "We are continuously reviewing our processes to ensure they are fair and transparent for all users."

The January policy supersedes an earlier version, from November 2024, which did not include the manual review step. That earlier version is no longer in effect, but several sellers told the Bulletin they were still receiving dispute outcomes based on the older criteria, suggesting the platform may not have fully updated its systems.

"The notice said the policy was changing, but the outcome letters I received still referenced the old wording," said a seller from Brighton who asked not to be named. "It's like they updated the document but not the software that generates the decisions."

The platform's own data, published in its most recent quarterly transparency report, shows a sharp increase in dispute activity. In the October to December quarter, the platform reported 1,842 disputes involving EasyShip labels, up from 617 in the previous quarter. Of those, 1,204 were resolved in favour of the buyer. The report notes that the figures are "subject to revision" and that "some dispute categories may overlap."

The January to March figures are not yet public. The platform said they would be released in the coming weeks.

Local sellers say the financial impact has been significant. The Bulletin surveyed 47 sellers in the Bayside area who reported experiencing at least one fraudulent dispute in the past six months. Combined, they said they had lost more than $38,000 in goods and shipping costs. The median loss was $240 per incident, but several sellers reported losses exceeding $1,000 for higher-value items such as electronics and designer clothing.

One seller, a retiree from Sandringham who sells vintage cameras, said he lost a $1,400 lens to a dispute that was approved within 48 hours of the parcel being collected.

"I had the tracking number, I had the receipt, I had a photo of the parcel at the counter," he said. "None of it mattered. The system just looked at the buyer's claim and the tracking status and decided against me."

The retiree said he had since stopped selling items valued above $200. "It's not worth the risk," he said. "The platform's fees are high enough. If I have to absorb losses on top of that, I might as well take the items to a consignment shop."

**Bayside Bulletin**
**Fake Shipping Scams Hit Local Marketplace**
**Council backs consumer education push after shipping-label fraud wave**

*By Sarah Mitchell*
*Bayside Bulletin Reporter*
*December 14, 2024*

Bayside Council has voted unanimously to fund a $45,000 consumer education campaign targeting online marketplace scams, following a series of reports from local sellers who say they have been defrauded through fake shipping labels.

The decision, made at Tuesday night's council meeting, allocates funds for a six-month program that will include workshops, a dedicated information page on the council website, and printed guides distributed through libraries and community centres. The program will focus on helping residents recognise fraudulent tracking numbers and understand their rights when disputes arise.

Councillor Helen Tran, who moved the motion, said the council had a responsibility to act after hearing from dozens of constituents who had lost money.

"These are not sophisticated scams in the traditional sense," Cr Tran said. "They are using the platform's own systems against the seller. The buyer generates a label, the tracking shows a parcel has been collected, and then the buyer claims it never arrived. The seller is left with nothing."

The motion passed 9–0, with all councillors present voting in favour. It also calls on the state government to review consumer protections for online marketplace transactions, particularly around the use of third-party shipping labels.

Mayor James O'Connor said the council would work with local business groups and the Bayside Community Legal Centre to develop the program's content.

"We are not experts in online marketplaces, but we know how to reach people in this community," Mayor O'Connor said. "We will bring in people who understand the platforms and the scams, and we will make sure that information is available to everyone who needs it."

The education campaign is expected to launch in February 2025, with the first workshop scheduled for the Bayside Library in Sandringham. Further sessions are planned for Brighton, Hampton, and Beaumaris.

**Sellers describe ongoing losses**

The council decision comes as local sellers continue to report losses from fraudulent disputes. The Bulletin's survey of 47 sellers in the Bayside area found that combined losses exceeded $38,000 in goods and shipping costs over the past six months.

Several sellers who attended Tuesday's meeting spoke during public question time, describing similar experiences: a buyer purchases an item, generates a shipping label through the platform's EasyShip service, and then claims the item never arrived. The tracking number shows the parcel was collected, but the seller says they never handed over the goods.

One seller from Elwood, who asked to be identified only as "Maria", said she had lost more than $600 on two separate transactions in November.

"The first time I thought it was a mistake," she said. "The second time I realised it was a pattern. The buyer had a new account, the address was a parcel locker, and the tracking showed the parcel was collected within an hour of the order. No one moves that fast."

Maria said she had since started recording video of every parcel before it was collected, but she was unsure whether the platform would accept the footage as evidence.

**Platform response under scrutiny**

The platform has said it is aware of the issue and has "updated its systems" to address fraudulent shipping labels. However, sellers say the changes have not resolved the problem.

A seller from Brighton, who asked not to be named, told the Bulletin that the platform's notification about the policy change did not match the outcome letters she received.

**Bayside Bulletin: Fake Shipping Scams Hit Local Marketplace**

**Consumer guide offers step-by-step protection as scams persist**

The Bayside Council has released a practical consumer guide to help residents spot and avoid fake shipping scams on online marketplaces, following months of complaints from local sellers and buyers.

The guide, published on the council's website and available in print at the Bayside Library, covers the most common scam patterns reported in the area. It walks readers through what to check before handing over goods, how to read tracking information critically, and what evidence to keep if a transaction goes wrong.

Council community safety officer Priya Sharma said the guide was written in plain language after feedback that earlier advice was too technical.

"People told us they wanted something they could print out and keep by their computer," Sharma said. "So we've made it very practical. It tells you exactly what to look for, step by step."

The guide lists several red flags that have appeared repeatedly in local reports. These include buyers who insist on using the platform's EasyShip service but then claim the parcel never arrived, tracking numbers that show collection within an hour of the order being placed, and accounts that were created only days before the purchase.

It also advises sellers to photograph or video every parcel before collection, to keep all messages within the platform's chat function, and to request signature on delivery where the service allows it.

**Local reactions mixed**

Residents who spoke to the Bulletin after the guide's launch said they welcomed the information but questioned whether it would be enough.

Maria, the Elwood seller who lost more than $600 across two transactions in November, said the guide was a good start but that the platform needed to do more.

"I've read the guide and it's clear, but it's telling me things I already know now," she said. "The problem is that the scammers know these systems better than we do. They change their methods. A printed guide can't keep up with that."

Another seller from Hampton, who asked to be identified only as "James", said he had stopped using the platform's shipping service altogether.

"I just use my own courier now," he said. "It costs a bit more, but at least I know the parcel is actually going to the buyer. I'd rather pay extra than lose the whole sale."

The guide also includes a section for buyers, warning them about sellers who ask for payment outside the platform or who send links to fake payment pages. Council staff said these reports had increased in recent months, though exact figures were still being compiled.

**Platform cooperation**

A spokesperson for the marketplace platform said the company had reviewed the guide and was "broadly supportive" of its content. The spokesperson said the platform had already updated its systems to address fraudulent shipping labels and encouraged users to report suspicious activity through its in-app tools.

However, the spokesperson did not respond to questions about whether the platform would change its dispute resolution process, which several local sellers have criticised.

The Brighton seller who previously told the Bulletin that the platform's notification about its policy change did not match the outcome letters she received said she had not seen any improvement.

"I got another letter last week saying my claim was closed because the tracking showed delivery," she said. "But the tracking was generated by the buyer. I never handed over the parcel. The system still doesn't seem to understand that."

**Council plans further sessions**

The education campaign will continue through March and April, with workshops scheduled at the Bayside Library in Sandringham on 12 March, followed by sessions in Brighton on 26 March, Hampton on 9 April, and Beaumaris on 23 April.
